questions.q: What is the actual root cause of Atlas's release delays, per this lesson?
options: Three teams with genuinely different release cadences and risk profiles are being forced through one shared pipeline, creating team-level collisions
Atlas has too many admins with production access
Atlas's Full sandbox has never been refreshed
Their single testing sandbox is too small in storage
questions.explain: The problem is a mismatch between three teams' different cadences and one shared, serialized pipeline -- not a sizing problem that adding one more sandbox would fix.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say "just add another sandbox" would not actually solve Atlas's problem?
options: Because Salesforce limits orgs to a maximum of two sandboxes total
Because adding sandboxes is technically impossible once an org exceeds 100 users
Because it would just move the collision point rather than removing it, since the underlying issue is unrelated work sharing a single serialized path to production
Because sandboxes cannot be created for financial services orgs
questions.explain: Lesson 13 solved a sizing problem by right-sizing one pipeline; Atlas's problem is different in kind -- it needs separate lanes for separate teams, not more capacity added to the same shared lane.

questions.q: What does a multiple-pipeline strategy give each team or release cadence, per this lesson?
options: A shared single environment that all teams use in strict rotation
Permanent, unrestricted access to every other team's environments
Its own full promotion path -- its own development, testing, and often staging tier -- that only converges with other pipelines near production
A separate production org for each team
questions.explain: Each pipeline runs independently on its own cadence, with convergence only happening at the very end, right before production -- not a separate production org, and not full cross-team access.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say two pipelines can each independently pass their own staging and still conflict once they reach production together?
options: Because staging environments are never accurate representations of production

Because each pipeline's testing only validates its own changes in isolation -- it can't detect an interaction between two different pipelines' changes that only becomes visible once both are combined in production
Because Salesforce randomly corrupts data during multi-pipeline deployments
Because staging sign-off is purely a formality with no real validation behind it
questions.explain: Commercial lending's required-field change and digital channels' Flow that skips that field could each be fine in isolation -- the conflict only appears once both land in production together, which neither pipeline's independent staging could have caught alone.

questions.q: What is a "release train," as this lesson defines it?
options: A physical data center where Salesforce servers are housed
An automatic rollback mechanism triggered whenever two pipelines disagree
A naming convention for sandboxes used only by the digital channels team
A coordinated schedule where multiple pipelines' changes are reconciled and sequenced before they all reach production together
questions.explain: A release train is the explicit coordination point large orgs with multiple pipelines need, so pipelines don't each assume they're the only one changing anything before reaching production together.
